symptom: a painless lump in the side of the neck for a year
hook: a tumour had pried the carotid fork apart like the arms of a lyre
whatYouSee: A round vascular tumour at the right carotid fork splays the internal and external carotid arteries apart like a lyre.
whyItMatters: A carotid body tumour is a paraganglioma of the chemoreceptor at the carotid bifurcation. It is a firm pulsatile swelling that may have a thrill and a bruit. Angiography shows splaying of both carotids called the lyre sign.
treatment: Treatment is usually surgical excision. Preoperative embolisation may be used to reduce bleeding.
takeaway: A vascular mass splaying the carotid fork is a carotid body tumour.

findings: Lateral projection digital subtraction-style catheter angiogram of the neck and skull base, with the face facing right and cervical spine on the left.
Contrast fills the common carotid artery, which bifurcates in the upper neck.
A well-circumscribed, round hypervascular tumor blush with dense, tangled fine vessels sits at the carotid bifurcation.
The mass splays the internal and external carotid arteries apart, widening the bifurcation (lyre-sign configuration).
Multiple small feeding branches, likely from the ascending pharyngeal and external carotid branches, supply the lesion.
The posterior vessel, probably the internal carotid, is displaced posteriorly and appears tortuous, without a clear occlusion or flow-limiting stenosis.
The anterior vessel, probably the external carotid, is bowed anteriorly around the mass and gives off branches.
The upper image shows a branching network of external carotid branches and an upper vascular blush near the skull base or occipital region.
Overlying bones include the mandible, teeth, and cervical vertebrae.
differential: Other hypervascular carotid space mass, such as glomus vagale paraganglioma or a vascular schwannoma/metastasis
Arteriovenous malformation or hypervascular vascular tumor near the bifurcation
anatomyConcerns: No impossible anatomy; the findings are consistent with a pathologic mass displacing normal vessels.
Vessel identification (internal versus external carotid) is inferred from branching pattern, as the full intracranial course is not shown.
Laterality cannot be determined from the image.

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: A round, well-circumscribed hypervascular blush with dense tangled fine feeding vessels sits at the carotid bifurcation and splays the internal and external carotid arteries apart (lyre sign). This is the classic discriminator for a carotid body tumour, and it fits the painless neck lump of one year. A glomus vagale paraganglioma would sit higher and displace the vessels differently, and a vascular schwannoma would be less vascular. Histology and laterality cannot be established from the image. The posterior vessel is tortuous, but this is plausible for an adult and is not an artifact. The projected mandible, teeth and cervical spine are coherent, and no lettering is present.
